headline: Strange New Energy Storage Could Power Half a Million Homes
meta_description: Freezing air to -321°F and heating industrial salt are solving renewable energy's biggest challenge: storage that lasts for weeks.
summary_short: Highview Power's Manchester project freezes surplus renewable energy into liquid air, storing enough power for 300 megawatts per hour—enough for nearly half a million ho…
body:
The race to power grids entirely on renewable energy has hit a fundamental obstacle: when the sun isn't shining and the wind isn't blowing, how do we keep the lights on? Two unusually ambitious projects now getting serious investment suggest the answer might be stranger than anyone expected. In Manchester, Highview Power's Carrington project freezes surplus renewable power to -321 degrees Fahrenheit, compressing air to just 1/700 of its original volume. When the grid needs power, the liquid warms and spins a turbine—with no combustion involved. The facility can store 300 megawatts per hour, enough to serve nearly half a million homes.

What sets liquid air apart from lithium-ion batteries is endurance. While lithium-ion handles hours of storage, liquid air can remain stable for days or weeks. This means during stretches of overcast or windless weather, the energy captured on sunny or breezy days remains available. In Nevada, a complementary approach uses a different strategy: 10,000 mirrors at the Crescent Dunes facility focus sunlight on industrial salts heated to 1,040 degrees Fahrenheit, holding that heat for extended periods.

These solutions represent a critical shift. Renewable energy generation has largely been solved, but storage has remained the missing piece—the problem that prevents truly round-the-clock clean power. By combining various storage technologies suited to different timescales and conditions, researchers are creating a more resilient energy system. Neither project relies on exotic materials or untested physics; instead, they use physics that sounds like science fiction precisely because it's so extreme—and that extremity is exactly what makes it work.
quick_facts: Highview Power freezes air to -321°F in Manchester, UK
300 megawatts per hour storage serves nearly half a million homes
Liquid air storage lasts days or weeks, unlike lithium-ion batteries
Crescent Dunes uses 10,000 mirrors to heat industrial salt in Nevada
